name: Cherry tomato
pet_note: ASPCA lists tomato plants as toxic to dogs and cats: leaves and stems contain solanine/tomatine; ripe fruit is low risk.
tip: Buy a sturdy transplant, set it deep up to the first leaves after nights stay above 50°F, and tie it to a 6-ft stake.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Slicing tomato
pet_note: ASPCA lists tomato plants as toxic to dogs and cats: leaves and stems contain solanine/tomatine; ripe fruit is low risk.
tip: Mulch and water deeply once a week, and remove lower leaves touching the soil to slow early blight, which is common in the Northeast.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Paste (Roma) tomato
pet_note: ASPCA lists tomato plants as toxic to dogs and cats: leaves and stems contain solanine/tomatine; ripe fruit is low risk.
tip: Determinate Romas ripen in a 3-4 week burst, so cage them and plan a canning or sauce day for late August.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Tomatillo
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA list, but it is a nightshade relative whose leaves and unripe fruit contain alkaloids; keep pets from chewing it.
tip: Plant at least two tomatillos because they need cross-pollination, and harvest when the fruit fills and splits the papery husk.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail

name: Jalapeño pepper
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; capsaicin in hot peppers can irritate a pet's mouth and stomach.
tip: Wait until soil is warm (about two weeks after last frost) to transplant, since cold soil stunts peppers for weeks.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Bell pepper
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Choose an early-maturing variety, use black plastic mulch to warm the soil, and expect fully red fruit to take 3-4 extra weeks past green.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Pickling cucumber
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Grow on a trellis for better airflow, pick every day or two at 3-4 inches, and watch for striped cucumber beetles in June.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Zucchini
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: One or two plants are plenty for a family; pick fruit at 6-8 inches every couple of days.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Butternut squash
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Give each vine about 16 sq ft, and harvest before the first frost once the rind is tan and can't be dented with a fingernail.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Pumpkin
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Count back from your first frost date (about 100 days) to sow, and slip a board under each fruit to prevent rot.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Sweet corn
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list (ASPCA's toxic 'corn plant' is a Dracaena houseplant); corn cobs are a serious intestinal blockage risk for dogs.
tip: Plant in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row so wind pollinates the ears fully.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Bush beans
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; cooked green beans are commonly fed to dogs, but raw dried bean seeds contain lectins.
tip: Sow seeds 1 inch deep once soil is warm, and pick pods while they are pencil-thin to keep plants producing.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Pole beans
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; raw dried bean seeds contain lectins, so don't let pets eat stored seed.
tip: Set up a 6-7 ft trellis or teepee before sowing, and keep picking every two days to extend the harvest into fall.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Sugar snap peas
pet_note: Garden peas are not on the ASPCA toxic list (unlike ornamental sweet pea, Lathyrus, which is toxic).
tip: Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early April, about four weeks before last frost, along a trellis at least 5 ft tall.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail

name: Lettuce
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Sow a short row every two weeks in spring and again in August, and harvest outer leaves so plants keep growing.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Spinach
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; spinach contains oxalates, so only small amounts are advised for pets.
tip: Sow 5 weeks before last frost because spinach bolts as days lengthen in June; a late-August sowing gives the best crop.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Kale
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Pick the lower leaves and leave the top growing, and use insect netting to keep cabbage worms off.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Swiss chard
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; chard contains oxalates, so only small amounts are advised for pets.
tip: Cut outer stalks at the base about an inch above the soil and the plant will keep producing from June until hard frost.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail

name: Arugula
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Sow small batches every two to three weeks in spring and fall; summer heat makes it bolt and taste hot.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail clamshells

name: Radish
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Thin seedlings to 2 inches apart and harvest within a week of maturity, before roots turn woody and split.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Carrot
pet_note: ASPCA lists carrot as non-toxic; a common dog treat.
tip: Keep the seedbed constantly moist for the 2-3 weeks carrots take to germinate (a board or burlap over the row helps), then thin to 2 inches.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Beet
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; no known toxicity, though large amounts of any plant can upset a pet's stomach.
tip: Each beet 'seed' is a cluster that sprouts several plants, so thin to one every 3 inches and eat the thinnings as greens.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail

name: Onion (from sets)
pet_note: Allium: ASPCA lists as toxic to dogs and cats (can damage red blood cells); keep pets out of the bed.
tip: Plant sets 1 inch deep in early spring, keep the bed weeded since onions can't compete, and harvest when the tops flop over.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Scallions (green onions)
pet_note: Allium: ASPCA lists as toxic to dogs and cats (can damage red blood cells); keep pets out of the bed.
tip: Sow thickly in a short row every 3-4 weeks; you can also regrow store-bought scallion roots in a glass of water on a windowsill.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail bunches

name: Garlic (fall-planted)
pet_note: Allium: ASPCA lists as toxic to dogs and cats (can damage red blood cells); keep pets out of the bed.
tip: Plant hardneck cloves 2 inches deep, pointy end up, around your first fall frost (4-6 weeks before the ground freezes), mulch with straw, and cut off the scapes in June.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; price est. from retail

name: Potato
pet_note: ASPCA lists potato as toxic to dogs and cats: green tubers, sprouts, and foliage contain solanine. Cooked ripe tubers are low risk.
tip: Plant certified seed potatoes, hill soil over the stems as they grow so tubers never see light, and hand-pick Colorado potato beetles.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Strawberry (day-neutral)
pet_note: ASPCA lists strawberry as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: Pinch off flowers for the first 4-6 weeks after planting, remove runners, and net the bed against birds once berries color.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension 'how much to plant per person' guides; USDA ERS Fruit & Vegetable Prices (2022 data, pub. 2023)

name: Basil
pet_note: ASPCA lists basil as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: Wait until nights stay above 50°F to plant, and pinch the tops weekly so plants bush out instead of flowering.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Cilantro
pet_note: ASPCA lists coriander (cilantro) as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: Cilantro bolts quickly in summer heat, so sow every 3 weeks in spring and again in late summer, in light afternoon shade.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Parsley
pet_note: ASPCA lists parsley as toxic to dogs and cats in large amounts: furanocoumarins can cause skin sensitivity to sunlight.
tip: Soak seeds overnight before sowing indoors because parsley is slow to germinate, or simply buy transplants.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Dill
pet_note: ASPCA lists dill as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: Sow directly where it will grow since dill dislikes transplanting, and leave a few plants to flower for swallowtail caterpillars and beneficial wasps.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Chives
pet_note: Allium: ASPCA lists as toxic to dogs and cats (can damage red blood cells); keep pets out of the bed.
tip: Snip leaves to 2 inches above the soil and they regrow all season; divide clumps every 3 years in spring.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Mint
pet_note: ASPCA lists mint (Mentha) as toxic to dogs and cats; it can cause vomiting and diarrhea.
tip: Grow mint in a pot (even a pot sunk into the bed) because its runners will take over a garden within a season.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Oregano
pet_note: ASPCA lists oregano as toxic to dogs and cats; it can cause mild vomiting and diarrhea.
tip: Plant in well-drained soil and full sun, and cut back by half in early summer for a fresh flush of flavorful leaves.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: Thyme
pet_note: ASPCA lists common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) as non-toxic; note 'Spanish thyme' (Coleus amboinicus) is a different, toxic plant.
tip: Give it sharp drainage (add grit or plant at a bed edge) because wet winter soil kills thyme more often than cold.
yield_source: Cornell/UMN Extension herb guidance; price est. from typical retail clamshell/bunch prices

name: German chamomile
pet_note: ASPCA lists chamomile as toxic to dogs and cats (vomiting, diarrhea; bleeding risk with long-term use).
tip: Press the tiny seeds onto the soil surface without covering them since they need light to germinate, and pick flowers when fully open.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail

name: Lemon balm
pet_note: ASPCA lists lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) as toxic to dogs and cats (vomiting, diarrhea); ASPCA also calls it 'bee balm', which is not Monarda.
tip: Shear plants before they set seed, because lemon balm self-sows aggressively much like its mint relatives.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail

name: Lavender (English)
pet_note: ASPCA lists lavender as toxic to dogs and cats (linalool can cause nausea and vomiting).
tip: Pick a hardy angustifolia variety like 'Munstead' or 'Hidcote', plant in gravelly well-drained soil, and never cut into bare woody stems.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail

name: Sunflower
pet_note: ASPCA lists sunflower as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost on the north side of the garden, and cover young seedlings if birds or squirrels dig them up.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail (seeds)

name: Zinnia
pet_note: ASPCA lists zinnia as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: The more you cut zinnias for bouquets, the more they bloom; water at the base to avoid powdery mildew.
yield_source: Not applicable (non-edible ornamental/cover crop)

name: Marigold (Tagetes)
pet_note: ASPCA lists marigold (Tagetes) as toxic to dogs and cats; sap can cause mild stomach upset and skin irritation.
tip: Tuck marigolds along the edges of the vegetable bed and deadhead spent flowers to keep color coming until frost.
yield_source: Not applicable (non-edible ornamental/cover crop)

name: Nasturtium
pet_note: ASPCA lists nasturtium as non-toxic to dogs and cats.
tip: Soak the large seeds overnight, sow after last frost in lean soil (rich soil means leaves, not flowers), and add the peppery flowers to salads.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail (edible flowers/leaves)

name: Cosmos
pet_note: Not found on the ASPCA toxic list; generally considered pet-safe, though not explicitly confirmed by ASPCA.
tip: Don't fertilize cosmos; it flowers best in average soil and may need a stake once it passes 4 feet.
yield_source: Not applicable (non-edible ornamental/cover crop)

name: Calendula (pot marigold)
pet_note: ASPCA lists calendula (pot marigold) as non-toxic to dogs and cats; don't confuse it with Tagetes marigolds.
tip: Sow around last frost, deadhead often, and cut plants back by a third in midsummer heat for a big fall rebloom.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail (edible petals)

name: Purple coneflower (Echinacea)
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; generally regarded as pet-safe.
tip: Plant nursery-grown native Echinacea purpurea in spring and leave the seedheads standing over winter to feed goldfinches.
yield_source: Not applicable (non-edible ornamental/cover crop)

name: Bee balm (Monarda)
pet_note: Monarda is not on the ASPCA toxic list; don't confuse it with lemon balm, which ASPCA also calls 'bee balm' and lists as toxic.
tip: Choose a mildew-resistant variety like 'Jacob Cline', give it good airflow, and divide clumps every 2-3 years.
yield_source: Estimate (no standard extension per-person guidance); price est. from specialty retail (tea/edible flowers)

name: Winter rye (cover crop)
pet_note: Not on the ASPCA toxic list; avoid letting pets graze seed heads, which can host toxic ergot fungus.
tip: Broadcast rye on empty beds in September or early October, then cut or turn it under in spring at least 3 weeks before planting.
yield_source: Not applicable (non-edible ornamental/cover crop)

name: Microgreens (indoor)
pet_note: Common microgreen mixes (radish, pea, sunflower, broccoli) are not on the ASPCA toxic list; avoid onion or chive microgreens around pets.
tip: Sow seeds thickly on moist potting mix in a shallow tray by a sunny window and snip with scissors when the first true leaves appear.
yield_source: One tray per person; price est. from retail microgreen clamshells
